say.text: A 58-year-old woman has a firm breast lump. Her core biopsy shows cells lying in single file, not in clumps.
Which histological type fits best?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what holds cells together in a mass. This type has lost that cell-to-cell glue, so its cells travel out one at a time.
The answer is invasive lobular carcinoma. Loss of the cell-adhesion protein E-cadherin lets the cells separate and lie in single file, not as one stellate mass.
Keep the cell pattern as your clue. How common a type is does not decide the answer.
That is not the right choice.
Ductal (NST) carcinoma is the commonest breast cancer, so it feels like the safe default. But it forms one hard, gritty, stellate mass, not cells in single file.
Read the cell arrangement before the frequency.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Commonest is a trap when the stem describes a pattern; the cell arrangement decides the type.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Medullary carcinoma is tempting because its lymphocytic infiltrate is prominent. But it is soft and well circumscribed, and its cells do not lie in single file.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Look at how the tumour cells are arranged, not at the stroma around them.

say.text: Which histological type is most often bilateral or multicentric?
That is not the right choice.
NST is so common that it wins by default. But this question asks about growth pattern, and NST forms one stellate mass.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the commonest type. For 'most often' questions, check how each type behaves.

say.text: The answer is invasive lobular carcinoma. It is the type most often bilateral and multicentric.
Its single-file cells also spread unusually, to peritoneum, ovaries, gut and meninges.
Which pair of chromosomal locations is correct for the two hereditary breast cancer genes?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Treat each gene as a separate fact with its own locus. Do not memorise the two numbers as one pair.
That is not the right choice.
The two numbers are easy to swap, because they are remembered as one pair. Each gene owns one locus, so hold the pairing gene by gene.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the numbers, which is exactly where the swap happens. Check each gene's own locus.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The two genes sit on different chromosomes, so placing both on 17q merges two separate loci.

sure_note.text: You were sure both genes share a site. Each gene has its own locus.

say.text: The answer is BRCA1 on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q.
For the numbers: BRCA1 is the 1, and it sits on 17. BRCA2 goes with 13.
A breast and ovarian cancer family carries a mutation on chromosome 17q. Which gene is most likely?
That is not the right choice.
BRCA2 is tempting because the two gene names and their numbers blur together. The stem names a chromosome, and each gene has only one.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the locus the stem names, not the gene you know better.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
PTEN belongs to Cowden syndrome, a real hereditary breast risk. But this stem describes the breast and ovarian BRCA pattern.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a syndrome gene. Check which family pattern the stem describes.

say.text: The answer is BRCA1. It lies on 17q, and BRCA1-linked cancers are typically triple-negative.
Next, the molecular subtype. Luminal A is the most common: oestrogen receptor (ER) or progesterone receptor (PR) positive, HER2 negative, with low Ki-67 (a proliferation marker).
Basal-like, or triple-negative, is ER, PR and HER2 negative. It is the pattern most linked to BRCA1.
A 3 cm tumour has peau d'orange over it, from blocked skin lymphatics, with no redness or warmth. Which T category does it give?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the skin sign alone shows. Then ask which T4 sub-category needs the whole red, warm, swollen picture.
That is not the right choice.
The inflammatory picture is tempting, since peau d'orange is the famous sign of inflammatory carcinoma. But the sign alone is only skin involvement.
T4d needs the whole red, warm, swollen breast, with one-third of it involved.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the sign. A single sign is not the whole syndrome; check the full clinical picture.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A skin sign does not show that the tumour is fixed to the chest wall. Fixity is tested with the pectoralis major contracted.

sure_note.text: You were sure of fixity. The skin sign and fixity are two separate findings; keep them apart.

say.text: The answer is T4b. Peau d'orange comes from blocked subdermal lymphatics with skin oedema, and on its own it places the tumour in T4b.
Lymph follows the same logic. About 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes, and most of the rest goes to the internal mammary nodes.
Axillary levels are set by pectoralis minor: level I lateral, level II behind it, level III medial. Ducts and fascia carry local spread, and Cooper's ligaments pull the skin into dimples.
Which gene is most associated with male breast cancer?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Klinefelter syndrome is the other male risk factor. Ask which BRCA gene the male pattern goes with, and set the other aside.
That is not the right choice.
BRCA1 is tempting because it is the best-known breast gene and answers most hereditary stems. But its typical cancers are triple-negative in women, a different pattern from male disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the best-known gene. Fame is not a reason to pick a gene for every phenotype.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
TP53 causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a real hereditary cancer risk, but it is not the link to male breast cancer.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a cancer gene. Name each gene with its own syndrome first, then match the phenotype.

say.text: The answer is BRCA2. It is the gene more associated with male breast cancer.
Klinefelter syndrome is the other risk factor, and male breast cancer is about 1% of all breast cancers.
Family A has triple-negative breast cancers in women. Family B has breast cancer in a man.
Which pairing of genes fits best?

choices.label: BRCA1 in family A, BRCA2 in family B

say.text: That is not the right choice.
BRCA1 for both is tempting, since it is the familiar gene. But breast cancer in a man does not fit the BRCA1 pattern of triple-negative cancers in women.

sure_note.text: You were sure one gene fits both families. Each family's pattern needs its own check.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Choosing BRCA2 for both is tempting if you stop at the male link. Family A's triple-negative cancers in women are not explained by that gene alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the male link. Check the other family's pattern before you apply it.

say.text: The answer is BRCA1 for family A, because its cancers are typically triple-negative. BRCA2 fits family B, the male breast cancer gene.
